Review an IUL you already own

To check an indexed universal life policy you already own, ask the insurer for an in-force illustration and read the guaranteed column first. It shows how long the policy stays in force at your current premium if only the guaranteed credits and charges apply. This page covers how to ask for one, what to check, and what a review can lead to.

Reviewed by Luay Sadqi, Licensed Agent · NPN 21370662 · Updated November 2026

What an in-force illustration is

An in-force illustration is the insurer’s updated projection of your own policy. It starts from today’s cash value, loan balance and premium, and shows the years ahead. The NAIC model rule on life insurance illustrations defines it as an illustration furnished after a policy has been in force for one year or more.

Your annual statement looks back at the past year. The illustration looks forward.

How to ask the insurer for one

  1. Find your policy number and the insurer’s service contact on your annual statement.
  2. Call or write as the policy owner. Ask for “an in-force illustration at my current premium.”
  3. Ask that it show guaranteed and non-guaranteed values year by year, with any loan included.

Under the model rule, the insurer furnishes one when the owner asks. Its notice to owners says you may ask once a year without charge. If nothing arrives within 30 days, it says to contact your state insurance department. States decide whether and how to adopt the model, so your state’s rule can differ.

Guaranteed and non-guaranteed columns

ColumnWhat it assumesHow to use it
GuaranteedOnly the values, credits and charges the policy guarantees.Read it first. Find the year it reaches zero.
Non-guaranteed (current)The current non-guaranteed credits and charges continue unchanged every year.Treat it as one possible path, not a promise.

The model rule puts guaranteed values first and shows a zero in any year with no guaranteed value. Non-guaranteed values must carry a statement that the insurer can change the assumptions and that actual results may be more or less favorable.

Four points for every IUL owner: The current cap and participation rate are non-guaranteed. The insurer can change them within the limits in your policy. Policy charges come out of the cash value. Surrender charges reduce what you receive if you cancel during the surrender period. The guaranteed column is only as strong as the insurer’s ability to pay claims.

Five questions to check

  1. Does the guaranteed column end, and when? Find the first year it shows zero. If that is earlier than you need coverage, ask what premium carries the policy to the age you choose.
  2. Is a loan balance growing? Compare the loan line on this year’s statement with last year’s. See how policy loans work.
  3. Is your premium below what was illustrated? Compare what you paid with your original illustration. The NAIC Life Insurance Buyer’s Guide says universal life lets you choose a flexible premium pattern as long as you pay enough to keep the policy in force.
  4. When do surrender charges end? Ask for the charge by policy year before any withdrawal, reduction or cancellation.
  5. What are the current cap and participation rate? Ask for today’s rates on each index account you use, and the minimums the policy allows.

A policy that needs attention does not mean anyone did something wrong.

What a review can lead to

We look first at ways to keep the policy you have.

  • Keep it and adjust the premium to a figure the insurer illustrates.
  • Lower the death benefit. If you need less coverage, ask the insurer to illustrate a smaller amount. Ask about any charge for the change, and about the tax test below.
  • Manage loans. Ask the insurer to illustrate paying loan interest, repaying part of a loan or pausing new loans.
  • In some cases, an exchange to another policy. This is a replacement. It is suitable only some of the time.
Before you replace a policy, including a 1035 exchange: A new policy has its own costs and its own surrender charge period, and the old policy may deduct surrender charges. A claim in a new policy’s first two years can be denied over inaccurate statements, and suicide limits can start again. If your health has changed, new coverage can cost more or be declined. State replacement rules apply. In Virginia, for example, 14VAC5-30 requires the agent to present a replacement notice, Form 30-A, read it to you unless you decline, and leave it with you. You get at least 10 days from delivery to examine the new policy. Paying for a new policy with money from the old one is a replacement too.

A review cannot promise a result. It lays out your options and their costs so you can decide. There is no fee for our help. If a new policy is placed through us, the insurer pays us a commission.

MEC and 1035 basics

General education, not tax advice. Ask a tax professional before you act.

  • Modified endowment contract (MEC). Under 26 U.S.C. 7702A, a policy entered into on or after June 21, 1988 is a MEC if it fails the 7-pay test. It fails when the amount paid in during the first 7 contract years is more than the law’s limit. Under 26 U.S.C. 72, a loan from a MEC is treated as a distribution.
  • Why it matters in a review. In the first 7 contract years, a large catch-up premium can cross that limit. Ask the insurer for your MEC limit before you send one. A cut in benefits in those years is tested as if the policy had been issued at the lower level.
  • 1035 exchange. Under 26 U.S.C. 1035, no gain or loss is recognized when a life insurance contract is exchanged for another life insurance contract. If you also receive money or other property, 26 U.S.C. 1031(b) says gain is recognized up to that amount. Ask how a policy loan is treated. A policy received in exchange for a MEC is a MEC. These are tax rules only. The cautions above still apply.

What to bring

  • Your annual statement.
  • The in-force illustration, if you have it. If not, we can help you word the request.
  • Your original sales illustration.
  • A record of premiums paid, and any loan statements.

You do not need to send health records, a Social Security number or a policy number to start. To ask for a review, use the IUL review form on this page, or first read how indexed universal life works.

Common questions

IUL Policy Review FAQ

What is an in-force illustration?
It is the insurer's updated projection of a life insurance policy you already own. It starts from today's cash value, loans and premium and shows future years in guaranteed and non-guaranteed columns. The NAIC model rule defines it as an illustration furnished after a policy has been in force for one year or more. For index-linked policies sold on or after December 14, 2020, NAIC guideline AG 49-A applies those illustration rules.
How do I get an in-force illustration for my IUL?
Call or write to the insurer's policy service office as the policy owner. Ask for an in-force illustration at your current premium, with any loan included. The NAIC model notice also lists contacting your agent. Under the NAIC model rule the insurer furnishes one when the owner asks. States decide whether and how to adopt the model, so your state's rule can differ.
Can an IUL lapse?
Yes. An IUL is a universal life policy, and the NAIC Life Insurance Buyer's Guide says universal life lets you choose a flexible premium pattern as long as you pay enough to keep the policy in force. An in-force illustration shows whether the guaranteed column reaches zero at your current premium, and in what year.
How do I know if my IUL is underfunded?
Compare the premium you pay with the premium in your original illustration. Then read the guaranteed column of a new in-force illustration. If it reaches zero earlier than you need coverage, ask the insurer what premium would carry the policy to the age you choose.
When do IUL surrender charges end?
It depends on your policy. Ask the insurer for the surrender charge by policy year. An illustration shows the value available on surrender after surrender charges, loans and loan interest, so you can see the difference year by year.
Should I replace my IUL with a 1035 exchange?
Only in some cases. A replacement brings new costs and a new surrender charge period. A claim in a new policy's first two years can be denied over inaccurate statements, and suicide limits can start again. A change in health can raise the cost or lead to a decline. State replacement rules, such as Virginia's, require a written notice first. Compare keeping and adjusting your current policy first. Tax points here are general education, not tax advice.
